passages.happening:
Paul opens the way letters of his day opened: who is writing, to whom, and a greeting. The writers are “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother” (verse 1). The letter goes to the church in Corinth and to all the believers in Achaia, the Roman province of southern Greece. Then the greeting: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 2).

Most of Paul's letters go on to thank God for the church. This one does not. Paul begins by praising God for what God has done for him, in trouble. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort” (verse 3).

He goes on: God is the one “who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God” (verse 4).

Then Paul links his own suffering with Christ's. “For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows” (verse 5). Whatever happens to Paul, it is for the church's good. If he is afflicted, it is for their comfort. If he is comforted, it is for their comfort too, so that they can endure the same kind of suffering (verse 6).

He ends with hope. “And our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Listen to how often one word comes back. In five verses, the word ‘comfort’, as a noun or a verb, is heard ten times. The Corinthians could not miss it. It is the first thing Paul wants them to hear.

The Greek word is paraklēsis. It comes from a verb meaning to call someone to your side. So comfort here is not a soft word, like a cushion. It means strength that comes from someone standing beside you: encouragement, courage, help to keep going. The same family of words gives the name ‘Paraclete’, used of the Holy Spirit in John's Gospel.

The word ‘troubles’ is the Greek thlipsis. It means pressure, being pressed hard, as grapes are pressed or as a weight presses down. Paul pairs the two words again and again. God does not always take the pressure away. He gives strength in it.

Paul's opening, ‘Blessed be’ God, would have sounded familiar to any Jew in the church. Many of Israel's prayers bless God in just this way, as several psalms do. Paul, a Jew, opens his most painful letter with praise.

Notice also what Paul does not do. In Corinth, a leader was expected to look strong. Paul's rivals there seem to have made much of their own power. Paul begins by telling the church that he has been crushed by trouble and needed comfort. He is not ashamed of it. He will build the whole letter on it.

And notice the direction comfort travels. It comes from God to Paul, and from Paul to the church, and from them to others. Comfort is not meant to stop with the person who receives it.

Finally, ‘the sufferings of Christ overflow to us’. Paul does not mean that Christ's death was not enough, or that believers add to it. He means that those who belong to Christ share his road. The world treated Jesus with hostility. It will treat his people the same way. But they share his life too, and so his comfort.
passages.ot:
Paul's opening blessing follows the pattern of Israel's prayers. A psalm ends, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen” (Psalm 41:13).

‘The Father of compassion’ recalls how God named himself to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

‘The God of all comfort’ is the God of the prophet Isaiah, who was told to bring comfort to a people in exile. “‘Comfort, comfort My people,’ says your God” (Isaiah 40:1). God says of himself, “I, even I, am He who comforts you” (Isaiah 51:12), and, “As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13).

The Psalms speak the same way about comfort in trouble. “This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life” (Psalm 119:50). “When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul” (Psalm 94:19). And in the darkest valley: “I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me” (Psalm 23:4). The comfort in that psalm is a presence, not an escape.
passages.hard:
Does this passage mean that suffering is good, or that God sends trouble so that we can comfort others?

No. Paul does not say that. He says God comforts his people in their troubles, and that comfort received can be passed on. That is a purpose God brings out of suffering. It is not a claim that the suffering itself is good, or that every hurt has been sent to teach a lesson. The Bible calls death an enemy, and Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). These verses do not ask anyone to call their pain a gift.

Nor do they ask anyone to be over their pain before they are ready to help someone else. Paul is not saying ‘get better so you can be useful’. He is saying that people who have been through trouble often know how to sit with others in it.

If you are in a hard place now, these verses do not ask you to feel comforted on demand. They tell you that God is called ‘the God of all comfort’, and that comfort often comes through people. If your trouble is heavy, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says comfort comes so that it can be passed on. Ask who has comforted you, and how: with words, or by staying near. Then ask who around you is in trouble now. You may not have answers for them. You may have something better: the comfort you were given, and the willingness to stand beside them.

passages.happening:
Now Paul tells the church something that had happened to him. “We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life” (verse 8).

He goes further. “Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (verse 9).

But God rescued him. “He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us” (verse 10).

And the church had a part in it: “as you help us by your prayers” (verse 11). When many pray and God answers, many will give thanks.
passages.hearers:
The province of Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of what is now Turkey. Its chief city was Ephesus, where Paul had worked for more than two years (Acts 19:10). But Paul does not say what happened, or exactly where.

Readers have made several guesses. The most common is the riot at Ephesus, when the silversmiths filled the theatre shouting for their goddess (Acts 19:23-41). Others point out that Acts does not say Paul's life was in danger then, and that Paul says ‘Asia’, not ‘Ephesus’. They suggest a severe illness, or an imprisonment that Acts does not tell, or some other danger. No one knows. The Corinthians may have known, and Paul did not need to explain.

What Paul does say is striking. ‘A burden far beyond our ability to endure.’ ‘We despaired even of life.’ ‘The sentence of death.’ The word for ‘despaired’ means to be utterly at a loss, with no way out. It is the same word Paul uses later when he says he is ‘perplexed, but not in despair’ (4:8). So Paul knew both: times when he was at a loss and still held on, and a time when he was past the end of his strength.

In Corinth, people expected a leader to look strong. Paul tells them he was crushed. He does not hide it or dress it up.

Notice too that he does not say he came through by his own courage. He says he learned not to trust in himself, ‘but in God, who raises the dead’. That is the God who raised Jesus. When Paul had nothing left, he looked to the one who brings life out of death.

And he asks for their prayers. Paul does not stand above the church as a man who needs nothing. He needs them. He wants them to pray, and then to give thanks together when God answers.
passages.ot:
‘God, who raises the dead’ is the God Israel knew as the giver of life. Hannah sang, “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6). Moses' song says, “I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

The Psalms often speak of being brought to the edge of death and rescued. “The ropes of death entangled me; the anguish of Sheol overcame me” (Psalm 116:3). “For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling” (Psalm 116:8). Sheol is the Hebrew word for the place of the dead. Jonah prayed, “From the belly of Sheol I called for help, and You heard my voice” (Jonah 2:2).

King Hezekiah once heard what sounded like a sentence of death. Isaiah told him, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover” (Isaiah 38:1). He prayed, and God gave him more years.

The Bible does not hide that God's people sometimes come to the end of themselves. Elijah sat under a tree and prayed that he might die (1 Kings 19:4). A psalm says, “In my alarm I said, ‘I am cut off from Your sight!’ But You heard my plea for mercy when I called to You for help” (Psalm 31:22).
passages.hard:
Paul himself says he was given more than he could bear. ‘We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure.’ Many people have been told that God never gives you more than you can handle. Paul says the opposite about his own life. The site's note on 1 Corinthians 10:13 explains that the verse people quote for that saying is about temptation to sin, not about suffering. Here Paul is honest that he came to the end of his strength.

So if your life feels like more than you can carry, that does not mean you are weak, or that your faith has failed. An apostle felt the same. And notice what Paul did not do. He did not carry it alone. He leaned on God, and he asked others to pray for him (verse 11). Later in this letter he tells how God comforted him through a friend who came (7:6).

Do not carry it alone either. Tell someone you trust today: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. Despair is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul learned in his darkest time to trust ‘in God, who raises the dead’. Ask where you have been trusting in yourself, and whether a hard season has shown you how little that can hold. Then ask who you can tell about your troubles, and whose troubles you could carry in prayer, as Paul asked the Corinthians to carry his.

passages.happening:
Now Paul begins to defend himself. Some in Corinth were saying he could not be trusted. He says his conscience is clear. He has behaved toward them with the sincerity that comes from God, “not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God” (verse 12). His letters mean what they say (verse 13).

Then he explains his travel plans. He had meant to visit them twice: “I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea” (verse 16). That did not happen. Was he careless? Does he say yes and mean no? “When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards, so as to say ‘Yes, yes’ when I really mean ‘No, no’?” (verse 17).

Paul answers by pointing past himself to God. “But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not ‘Yes’ and ‘No’” (verse 18). Jesus Christ, whom Paul, Silvanus and Timothy preached in Corinth, was not yes and no, “but in Him it has always been ‘Yes’” (verse 19). “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ. And so through Him, our ‘Amen’ is spoken to the glory of God” (verse 20).

It is God who makes them firm in Christ. “He anointed us, placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come” (verses 21-22).

Then Paul gives the real reason he did not come. “I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth” (verse 23). And he adds at once: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
In 1 Corinthians Paul had said he would come through Macedonia, the province to the north, and then to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:5). Later he seems to have changed that plan, and then changed it again. To the Corinthians, it may have looked as if he did not keep his word. In their world, a man's word was part of his honour. Someone who said yes and no at the same time, to keep his choices open, was thought unreliable. Paul's critics used it against him.

Paul does not answer by listing his reasons first. He talks about God. God is faithful. The message Paul preached was Jesus Christ, and Jesus is God's great ‘Yes’. If the message is that firm, the messenger is not playing games.

‘Amen’ is a Hebrew word that means ‘it is true’ or ‘so be it’. The church said it at the end of prayers, as Paul says here. When believers say Amen, they agree with God's yes.

Verses 21 and 22 use three pictures. To ‘anoint’ was to pour oil on someone to set them apart, as kings and priests were in Israel. The Greek word shares its root with ‘Christ’, which means the anointed one. A ‘seal’ was a mark pressed into wax to show who owned something or to show that a letter was genuine. And the ‘pledge’ is the Greek arrabōn. It was a business word, found in many old Greek papers, for a down payment: a first part of the price, paid now, that promises the rest will follow. Paul says God has given his Spirit as that first part. The Spirit is a real share now in the life to come, and God's promise that the rest will come.

Silvanus, in verse 19, is a fuller, Latin form of the name Silas. Most take him to be the Silas who was with Paul when the church in Corinth began (Acts 18:5).

Last, look at verse 24. Paul has real authority as an apostle. But he refuses to use it as a master over their faith. He calls himself their fellow worker, working ‘for your joy’.
passages.ot:
Paul's ‘as surely as God is faithful’ rests on the God of the Old Testament, who keeps his word. Moses said, “Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations” (Deuteronomy 7:9). And Balaam was made to say, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind” (Numbers 23:19).

‘All the promises of God’ include the promises to Abraham, to David and through the prophets. Paul says every one of them comes true in Jesus.

Jesus himself taught his followers to speak plainly: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). James repeats it (James 5:12).

The anointing recalls Israel's kings. When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13). The Old Testament joined anointing and the Spirit. And the word ‘pledge’ is used in Genesis, when Tamar asks Judah, “Only if you leave me something as a pledge until you send it” (Genesis 38:17). There the pledge was his seal, cord and staff, held until the promised payment came.

God had promised through Joel, “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28). For Paul, the Spirit in believers' hearts is that promise coming true.
passages.hard:
Does ‘all the promises of God are Yes in Christ’ mean God will give me whatever I ask for?

No. Some teaching uses this verse to say that believers can claim health, money or success, and that God must say yes. That is not what Paul means. ‘The promises of God’ are the promises God actually made in Scripture: to forgive, to be with his people, to raise the dead, to make all things new. Paul says they are sure because of Jesus.

Paul's own life shows the difference. In this same letter he tells how he asked three times for his ‘thorn in the flesh’ to be taken away, and God said no, and gave him grace instead (12:7-9). God's yes in Christ is a yes to his promises. It is not a yes to every wish.
passages.asks: Paul's word was questioned, and he pointed to God's faithfulness. Ask whether your own ‘yes’ can be trusted, at home, at work, with friends. Then ask what promises of God you are leaning on. And ask how you use whatever authority you have, as a parent, a leader or a friend: over people, or alongside them ‘for your joy’.
